bioghist.head: Historical Information
bioghist.p: Context for Record: A 1790 Act of Congress titled "An Act for the encouragement of learning, by securing the copies of maps, Charts, and books, to the authors and proprietors of such copies, during the times therein mentioned," directed clerks of the District Courts to keep a book in in the clerk's office for the purpose of recording copyrights filed in that district. The clerk would then give the author or proprietor of the work a copy under the seal of the court. In 1870, the rules and responsibilities of copyright transferred from the courts to the Library of Congress.

Locality History: Arlington County was originally named Alexandria County. It was formed from a portion of Fairfax County that Virginia in 1789 ceded to the federal government for use as the site of a new national capital. In 1801 the area officially became part of the District of Columbia, although Congress named it Alexandria County. By an act of 9 July 1846, Congress returned the county to Virginia, and the General Assembly extended the commonwealth's jurisdiction over the region effective 20 March 1847. By an act of assembly passed 16 March 1920, the county's name was changed to Arlington, the name of the Custis family mansion (the home of Robert E. Lee), which is located in the county. An urban county, Arlington contains no incorporated towns or cities.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content
scopecontent.p: Arlington County (Va.) Copyrights Rights Secured, 1802-1845, consists of a volume recording copyrights filed before the District Court clerks, Edmond Lee and later Cassius F. Lee, of the District of Columbia.

The volume begins with an alphabetical index and then records individual copyrights. The copyrights note the name of the individual filing, the date copyright was secured, and the title of the work. Some entries include notations documenting the date the original work was filed with the State Department. The volume contains 219 leaves.
